heritage.name: Gimhae Kim clan
heritage.homeland: Gimhae, South Gyeongsang Province, southeastern Korea
heritage.migrationStory: Branches spread from southeastern Korea throughout the peninsula over many centuries. Some descendants later joined Korean migration to China, the Russian Far East, Japan and the Americas.
heritage.funFact: This is Korea’s largest Kim clan, and its traditional founder is King Suro of Gaya.

research.meaning: The surname is written with 金, the Chinese character meaning “gold” or “metal.” In Korean, this character is pronounced Gim when used as this surname, although Kim is the established international spelling.
research.summary: Kim is South Korea’s most common surname, borne by about one in five people in the 2015 census. It includes many distinct ancestral clans, identified by a bon-gwan—an ancestral seat—rather than descending from one shared founder.
research.originStory: Two major Kim traditions trace their beginnings to ancient kingdoms in southeastern Korea. The Gimhae Kim clan claims descent from King Suro, the legendary founder of Geumgwan Gaya in 42 CE, whose founding story describes golden eggs descending from heaven. The Gyeongju Kim clan traces its ancestry to Kim Alji, reportedly discovered in a golden chest in a forest in 65 CE; his descendants later ruled Silla. These are treasured foundation legends, not independently verified accounts.

timeline.event: King Suro establishes Geumgwan Gaya at present-day Gimhae; Gimhae Kim genealogies identify him as their founder.
Kim Alji’s discovery in a golden chest becomes the founding legend of the Gyeongju Kim clan.
Beginning with King Naemul, Kim rulers dominate Silla’s monarchy until the kingdom’s surrender to Goryeo.
Korean migrants, including Kim families, settle in the Russian Far East, China and Hawaii; organized Korean immigration to Hawaii begins in 1903.
Soviet authorities forcibly deport approximately 172,000 ethnic Koreans from the Russian Far East to Central Asia, including many Kim families.
Migration expands Korean communities in North America, Europe and elsewhere; South Korea’s 2015 census records approximately 10.7 million people surnamed Kim.

heritageOptions.name: Gyeongju Kim clan
heritageOptions.homeland: Gyeongju, North Gyeongsang Province—the former Silla capital
heritageOptions.migrationStory: Branches dispersed across Korea during the Goryeo and Joseon periods. In modern times, descendants also joined wider Korean migration to Japan, North America and other destinations.
heritageOptions.funFact: Gyeongju’s Gyerim grove is associated with the legend of the clan ancestor Kim Alji.

heritageOptions.name: Gwangsan Kim clan
heritageOptions.homeland: Gwangsan, in present-day Gwangju, southwestern Korea
heritageOptions.migrationStory: Branches established homes beyond their ancestral seat, including in the Chungcheong region, during the Joseon period. Modern descendants have also settled overseas through the broader Korean diaspora.
heritageOptions.funFact: The influential Joseon scholar Kim Jang-saeng belonged to this clan.

funFacts: Sharing the surname Kim does not automatically mean two people belong to the same ancestral clan.
A bon-gwan names an ancestral seat, not necessarily a person’s birthplace or current home.
Korean names traditionally place the family name first, so Kim comes before the given name.
The same character 金 is usually pronounced geum when it means gold in ordinary Korean vocabulary.
South Korea’s Constitutional Court ruled against the same-surname, same-clan marriage prohibition in 1997; current restrictions focus on close kinship.
research.caveat: Kim strongly suggests Korean heritage, but the spelling alone cannot identify your clan or establish ancestry. Your family’s bon-gwan, genealogical register (jokbo), or older family records would help distinguish the many Kim lineages; Kim also occurs in other naming traditions, including Vietnamese.

outline.title: The Fish That Carried Home
outline.tagline: Two brass halves carry Joon through a century of leaving—and belonging.
outline.logline: When sixteen-year-old Joon Kim discovers half a brass fish in Toronto, it pulls him into a fictional family's journey rooted in the real history of Korea and Korean migration to Canada. To return home, he must follow successive generations from Gimhae through occupation, war, and resettlement—and discover why someone cut their family treasure in two.

heirloom.name: The Split Brass Fish
heirloom.description: A palm-sized brass fish with hand-punched scales, a round eye, and 김해 scratched beneath its belly; Joon finds only the head half, hanging from a faded blue cord. Made as a personal family keepsake rather than a traditional clan artifact, it warms whenever a descendant tells its story and carries Joon forward to another moment in its history. Joining it to its missing tail will take him home.

outline.mystery: Why was the brass fish cut in half?

cast.name: Dae Kim
cast.role: Joon's great-great-grandfather; a Gimhae metalworker and the fish's maker
cast.look: Twelve in 1894, twenty-eight in 1910, and sixty-eight in 1950; lean, with a long face, prominent ears, and a crescent scar on his left thumb. His straight black hair becomes silver; a patched indigo work vest remains his visual signature.

cast.name: Sun Kim
cast.role: Dae's daughter and Joon's great-grandmother; the ancestor Joon bonds with most closely
cast.look: Twenty-eight in 1950, twenty-nine in 1951, and fifty-two in 1974; short and sturdy, with broad cheekbones and a straight black bob that later grays. Wears a mustard cardigan and carries a rectangular wooden sewing box.

cast.name: Min Kim
cast.role: Sun's son and Joon's grandfather; a refugee child who later immigrates to Toronto
cast.look: Four in 1950, five in 1951, and twenty-eight in 1974; round-faced, with large dark eyes and an unruly forelock. A blue cloth scarf follows him from childhood into adulthood; in Toronto he wears a brown corduroy jacket.

cast.name: Aunt Hana
cast.role: Joon's aunt in Toronto; keeper of the family's surviving objects
cast.look: Fifty-four, tall, with a square jaw, silver-streaked black hair in a low bun, red rectangular glasses, and a green knitted vest with oversized pockets.

acts.title: A Fish Without a Tail
acts.beat: Helping Aunt Hana sort family belongings, Joon—short black hair, round glasses, headphones around his neck—finds half a brass fish beside an incomplete genealogy identifying the family's bon-gwan as Gimhae. When he asks why the fish was cut, it burns warm and drops him into a Gimhae workshop, leaving him with one clear goal: find its missing tail and get home.
acts.history: A bon-gwan identifies an ancestral seat rather than a person's birthplace, and sharing the surname Kim does not establish membership in the same clan.

acts.title: Gold Is Not a Crown
acts.beat: Joon meets twelve-year-old Dae, who makes the fish from a scrap of brass while helping in a metalworking shop, and earns his trust by rescuing the unfinished keepsake from spilled charcoal. Near the traditionally identified tomb of King Suro, Dae shares the golden-egg founding story; Joon initially expects royal treasure, but discovers that this family's precious inheritance is skilled work and a story of belonging.
acts.history: Gimhae Kim genealogies traditionally trace their origin to King Suro's foundation of Geumgwan Gaya in 42 CE, but the golden-egg account is a foundation legend rather than independently verified history.

acts.title: The Road to the Port
acts.beat: The fish carries Joon to grown-up Dae, whose small workshop cannot reliably support his household and who seeks repair work in nearby Busan as Japan formally annexes Korea. Joon helps save Dae's tools from a rain-swollen stream on the road, but their arrival brings a harder discovery: changing addresses cannot shield the family from colonial rule.
acts.history: Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled it until 1945, while Busan's expanding colonial port economy drew workers from surrounding districts.

acts.title: A Bridge Behind Them
acts.place: Seoul, then roads south toward Busan
acts.beat: The next jump reveals that Dae's family moved to Seoul for work in the 1930s; now Joon joins Dae, Sun, and little Min in fleeing the Korean War, with the destroyed Hangang bridge cutting off their intended crossing. Crowded roads, scarce food, and advancing armies force repeated detours, and during a chaotic separation Joon loses sight of Dae—then notices that Sun is carrying only the fish's head.
acts.history: The Korean War began on June 25, 1950, and South Korean forces destroyed the Hangang bridge on June 28 while civilians were still fleeing Seoul.

acts.title: A Home Made of Scraps
acts.beat: In crowded wartime Busan, Sun repairs clothes near Gukje Market while Joon watches Min and helps turn discarded fabric into saleable garments, but every family search ends without certain news of Dae. When a relief worker delivers Dae's tool roll and a sealed packet from another refugee, Sun recognizes her father's scar-marked hand in a sketch enclosed with it and puts the packet into her sewing box without opening it.
acts.history: Busan served as South Korea's wartime capital and sheltered large numbers of refugees, while markets such as Gukje became important places for trading scarce goods.

acts.title: Another Shore, Another Workshop
acts.beat: Joon follows adult Min and Sun to Toronto, where Min's immigration application has been accepted but unfamiliar English, rejected work experience, and expensive housing make starting over difficult. As they repair secondhand furniture and take garment work, Joon spots the same sealed packet in Sun's sewing box; before he can open it, the fish pulls him into a final overlapping glimpse of that box in Aunt Hana's present-day home.
acts.history: Canada introduced its immigration points system in 1967, and Korean immigration expanded during the following decades, helping establish communities including Toronto's.

acts.title: Two Pieces, One Promise
acts.era: Present day, with a final glimpse of 1950
acts.beat: Still caught between times, Joon guides Hana to the sewing box, where the packet contains the missing tail and Dae's note: he cut the fish before their dangerous journey so that he and Sun could each carry a piece, promising to join them when they found one another again; another refugee returned his half after his death. Joon reunites the pieces and returns fully home, understanding that the promise survived even though Dae did not, then helps Hana record their family's story with its uncertainties intact.
acts.history: Family letters, objects, and oral histories can preserve experiences absent from official records, but a clan genealogy alone cannot verify an individual family's migration story.

historyNote.title: Did you know? A surname needs context
historyNote.body: A Korean bon-gwan identifies a clan's ancestral seat, not necessarily where a person was born. Gimhae is the ancestral seat of the Gimhae Kim clan. People who share the surname Kim can belong to different clans. The brass fish and this family's time-travel story are fictional.

dialectWord.meaning: A clan's ancestral seat, often named for a place.

quiz.explanation: An ancestral seat connects a clan to a place, even when its members live elsewhere.

historyNote.title: Did you know? A king from an egg
historyNote.body: Gimhae Kim genealogies traditionally name King Suro as their founder. Tradition dates his founding of Geumgwan Gaya, centered at present-day Gimhae, to 42 CE. The golden-egg account is a founding legend, not independently verified history. Dae and his handmade brass fish are fictional parts of this adventure.

quiz.question: How should we understand King Suro's golden-egg story?
options: As proof that royal gold lies beneath the tomb
As a founding legend passed down through generations
As instructions for making a brass fish
quiz.explanation: The golden-egg story is a founding legend, not an independently verified account.
